# Do predictor transformations matter?

**Bottom line.**  Averaged over the four economies and four horizons, the current features (0.827 of the no-change error) beat every alternative: full transform library 0.833, best three per variable 0.844, lags 1-12 of current 0.847, best transform per variable 0.848, core-anchored target 0.869.  Anchoring the target on core inflation helps two years out (3 of 4 economies) but hurts at short horizons in the euro area and Japan, where energy swings dominate.

Every raw predictor got a library of candidate transformations (50,440 candidates over four economies and four horizons; 293 exact aliases of the benchmark dropped).  Each was added to the own-inflation benchmark and scored out of sample in real time: chosen on forecast origins 2000-2010, judged on origins from 2013.

## One variable at a time

* **Early winners do not stay winners.**  The best transformation of each variable on 2000-2010 beat the benchmark on 2013-2026 in 36% of cases; a random candidate did so in 36%.
* **Significance does not persist.**  Of the 8,190 candidates significant on 2000-2010 (Clark-West, 5% one-sided), 18% were significant again on 2013-2026, against 14% of all candidates.
* **Re-choosing every month does not help.**  Picking each variable's transformation by its track record to date gave a positive holdout gain for 35% of variables.

| 24 months | 2.36 | 2.49 | 1.70 |

## Stickiness check for the current US forecast

In the 84 US months since 1960 when headline inflation ran at least 0.9 points above core during an oil surge of 25% or more, inflation fell a median 0.9 points over the next year; it fell 2 points or more 31% of the time, and core moved a median +0.2 points.  In 2026-10 headline was 3.9%, core 2.8% and oil +40% on the year.
